html:
The Corded Ware culture was a wide archaeological culture of northern and central Europe, from about 2900 to 2300 BCE, stretching from the Rhine to the Volga. It is named after pottery decorated by pressing cord into wet clay.

Its people buried their dead singly under small mounds, often with stone battle-axes. Ancient DNA shows they carried much ancestry from the steppe herders of the Yamnaya culture, mixed with that of earlier farmers, which points to a large movement from the steppe around 3000 BCE; see Yamnaya expansion. Many scholars link it to the spread of Indo-European languages.

It fed into the Bell Beaker culture in the west and the Únětice culture of the Bronze Age, and a move east toward the Urals helped form the Sintashta and Andronovo cultures.
